meta.title: Who really said "Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wooden really did define success this way. But the exact sentence that circulates is not the one his own sourced quotations use.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is Wooden’s. The wording is a variant — and the only version Wikiquote sources reads differently.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Defining success against your own effort rather than against a scoreboard is the heart of Wooden’s teaching, and this sentence is the form that circulates. We could not tie that exact wording to a primary edition: Wikiquote’s only sourced version of the definition comes from a 2000 television interview and reads differently.

source.heading: The wording is the open question

docMeta.dd: Interview on Charlie Rose (2000), per Wikiquote

source.excerpt: Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable.
trail: Wooden is known for the “Pyramid of Success,” which framed success in life as well as in basketball — Wikipedia ↗.

Wikiquote’s John Wooden page ↗ groups his quotations under the works they come from. The definition of success is not among the lines it places in his books; the version it does source is the differently-worded one from the 2000 Charlie Rose interview.
Quote Investigator ↗ has traced six Wooden sayings. This is not one of them, so there is no specialist finding to defer to here.

Wooden’s memoir They Call Me Coach (1972) ↗ is catalogued at the Internet Archive but lending-restricted, so we could not read it to check the wording ourselves. We are not asserting it is absent — only that we did not confirm it.
source.excerptNote: That is the sentence in circulation. The closest wording Wikiquote attaches to an actual source reads: “Success is peace of mind attained only through self-satisfaction and knowing you’ve made the effort, do the best of what you’re capable.” — credited there to his 2000 interview on Charlie Rose. Same thought, different sentence.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of John Wooden and his publishers
source.rightsNote: Every documented published form of Wooden’s definition of success dates from well after 1930, so this text is treated as in copyright. We have not identified which publication the popular wording first appeared in, so no single rights holder can be named with confidence.

author.name: John Wooden
author.heading: About John Wooden
author.bio: John Robert Wooden won ten NCAA championships in twelve years at UCLA, including seven in a row, and was the first person inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame as both a player and a coach. He is remembered less for the trophies than for the teaching — short, plain maxims delivered to teenagers, and the “Pyramid of Success” he built around the idea that success is something you measure against yourself.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is fine. The sentence is the problem.
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this one. What is unresolved is whether Wooden ever wrote these particular words in this particular order.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ attaches a differently-worded definition to Wooden’s 2000 Charlie Rose interview: “Success is peace of mind attained only through self-satisfaction and knowing you’ve made the effort, do the best of what you’re capable.” The popular wording is smoother and is the one that spread.
Wooden’s books are the obvious place to look, and the 1972 memoir ↗ is lending-restricted at the Internet Archive. We could not read a primary edition, so we do not claim one.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Wooden’s and so is the framing — Wikipedia ↗ notes the Pyramid of Success measured success in life, not only in basketball. The exact sentence above is the form that travels; we could not pin it to an edition.

context.heading: Why the definition mattered
lead: Wooden was a high-school English teacher before he was a famous coach, and his definition of success is a teacher’s answer to a student’s question: how do you know if you did well? His reply moved the goalposts inward. Not the score, not the ranking — whether you made the effort to become the best you were capable of becoming.
That is why the sentence outlived the basketball. It travels into business books and graduation speeches because it hands you a standard nobody else gets to grade.
context.pull: It moves the goalposts inward: not the score, but the effort.
